subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: You mean after the private act was passed?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext: Quite, and we should make provision for it here in the broad public legislation dealing with the question of export. I entirely agree with the minister that our jurisdiction is only with respect to export. We have nothing to do with power qua power except such as is developed in the St. Lawrence, and we have something to say there because there is the question of navigation; but with respect to power created by private enterprise, the provinces have to deal with that. But we have trade and commerce under federal jurisdiction. What I cannot contemplate is that there should be no record of the authorization except the statute. There should be information that this licence is on record. But if we do not contemplate that, this section need not stand so far as I am concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY

speechtext: Could we not have all the amendments which the government now propose put in the votes and proceedings to-morrow, or read now on the record, so that we can consider them all?

present in force. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
That is pretty nearly
there now, in section 9.

subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Then, coming
to section 5, there is a similar amendment:
That section 5 be amended by inserting, immediately after the number 5 at the beginning of the section and before the word "section," the following words:
"subject as hereinafter in this act provided."
For that the explanation is similar to what I have already given.
That section 9 of the bill be struck out and the following substituted therefor:

"11. Nothing in this act contained shall affect any licence existing at the date of the commencement of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act Amendment Act, 1938, and every such licence may notwithstanding the repeal of any of the provisions of this act by the said Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act Amendment Act, 1938, be renewed from time to time or revoked by the governor in council in the like manner and circumstances and with the like result and subject to the like terms and conditions as if such provisions had not been repealed but remain in force."

subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY

subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY

subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY

With regard to section 6 of the bill, which provides a new subsection 2 for section 8 of the act, I can find no authority for parliament to enact such a section unless as preliminary thereto parliament declares such lines, wires, conductors, and contrivances to be "works for the general advantage of
Canada". The only way in which it is possible,
1	believe, for parliament to obtain legislative jurisdiction over the lines running through any province is by declaring them to be "works for the general advantage of Canada," and I should like the minister to consider an amendment to section 8, the first subsection to read something like this:
(1)	All transmission lines or lines of wire or other conductors for the exportation of power and all pipe lines and other like contrivances for the exportation of fluid, from any place in Canada to any place outside of Canada, are hereby declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada.
I think that might be followed by a subsection which is contained in the bill-

The suggestion of my hon. friend recommends itself

6. Section 8 of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
8. (1) All transmission lines or lines of wire or other conductors for the exportation of power and all pipe lines and other like contrivances for the exportation of fluid, from any place in Canada to any place outside of Canada, are hereby declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada.
(2)	Subject to any regulation of the governor in council in that behalf, the governor in council may grant licences for the construction, placing or laying of any transmission line or line of wire or other conductor for the exportation of power, or of any pipe line or other like contrivance for the exportation of fluid.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister Of Pensions and National Health) moved the second reading of Bill No. 35, to amend the War Veterans' Allowance Act.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
Before the bill is given second reading, perhaps it would be in order to congratulate the minister upon having awakened the government, this sleeping giant of a government, long enough for it to do something about the problem of the 5,100 odd unemployed veterans with service in an actual theatre of war who were found by the veterans' assistance commission to be wholly or partly unfit to work. I believe the minister will admit that in the

task of rousing this sleeping giant he has been aided by some gentle prodding by members on this side of the house and also by a most emphatic recommendation from the veterans' assistance commission, which will be found at page 69 of their report, as follows:
Unfit Veterans
That the War Veterans' Allowance Act be amended by removal of "age 55 years," where it refers to the granting of an allowance because of disability, preaging and general unfitness;
And further:
That the act be amended so as to permit a more liberal interpretation of legislation covering the granting of the allowance at any age to a veteran who saw service in a theatre of actual war and who, because of his unfit condition, or other handicaps, is unable to maintain himself.
As the house will see, that was a most emphatic recommendation; but I am afraid, from what the minister said the other day, that this sleeping giant rolled over and went to sleep again before the minister was able to get him to do anything about the 10,000 unemployed veterans who served in a theatre of war and who are fit. It appeared from the minister's remarks that nothing was to be done about these 10,000 fit veterans.
If it is intended to cover all the 5,100 odd wholly or partly unfit veterans, then probably everyone in the house will agree with the principle of this bill, and the minister himself, speaking the other day, said that such was the case. His remarks will be found at page 1041 of Hansard where he is reported as follows:
All those who are partially fit or unfit will be looked after under the provisions of this legislation.
If that is the intention of the government, we can all approve of the bill; but there are one or two reservations I should like to make. In the first place, it seems to me that in the new section 4 an element of permanency is introduced. As the minister knows, our amendment in 1936 provided that veterans of a certain class need only be temporarily incapable of maintaining themselves; they did not have to be permanently disabled. In this section, however, we find the words, "and unlikely to become capable of maintaining himself," which I am afraid may be interpreted as adding a feature of permanency, which would mean that a veteran must be permanently disabled. As against that, the veterans' assistance commission have recommended that the men be given every incentive to get work and to reestablish themselves and get off the allowance. I suggest that the section should be amended to make it quite clear that the veteran, in order to get the

War Veterans' Allowance Act
allowance, need not be permanently disabled. Further the resolution which was passed the other day and on which this bill is based did not mention anything of that kind but simply referred to those "incapable of maintaining themselves," although the minister himself, speaking in reference to these men, said that they should be men who would not likely again become self-supporting. In my opinion it would be unwise to restrict this new classification in that way.
Another feature of the bill which should be looked into carefully is the provision that if the recipient is drawing old age pension he cannot get the war veteran's allowance. The minister may be quite right in his amendment on this point, but I hope the effect will not be to enable the government or the war veterans' allowance board to force veterans onto the old age pension. After all, they prefer to get the war veterans' allowance. The benefits under the War Veterans' Allowance Act are greater than benefits under the Old Age Pensions Act:	for example, a
veteran's widow can get an allowance for a year after the veteran's death under the War Veterans' Allowance Act, but that is not the case under the Old Age Pensions Act; then under the War Veterans' Allowance Act the soldier may have a home of a value of 82,000 without its -being taken into consideration in setting his allowance, which also is not the case under the Old Age Pensions Act, and there are several other respects in which it is of much more benefit to come under the War Veterans' Allowance Act than under the Old Age Pensions Act. This particular section of the bill dealing with the Old Age Pensions Act should be carefully considered.
Then I have a new suggestion to make in regard to the War Veterans' Allowance Act. We have now had experience for several years in the administration of the act, and there are many instances in which recipients of a war veteran's allowance are unable to get medical treatment. These men are indigents; they have no money to go to a doctor or a hospital or to get dental treatment. I suggest that it would be wise if the government at this time took steps to provide for giving some hospitalization and medical and dental treatment to recipients of the war veterans' allowance. It might mean that if a man were treated he could go out and earn his own living and go off the allowance, whereas at present he probably cannot get treatment at all unless he gets it from the city authorities, and in many instances gets worse and worse and has no chance whatever of getting off the allowance.
I think the same thing applies to pensioners. Our pension law at the present time requires proof of pensionable disability. We have seventy or eighty thousand soldiers who have suffered gunshot wounds but are not drawing pension at all; many of them have never applied for pension; yet if they have trouble with their wounds they cannot get treatment unless they can prove that they are suffering from a pensionable disability, which means that they must put all the expensive pension machinery to work to prove entitlement to a pension, whereas all they really want is treatment. I think the time has come when the government of Canada should give serious consideration to this whole question of medical and dental treatment, and hospitalization. In that connection I would refer again to the report of the commission, a significant finding. At page 35 they say:
We were much impressed on the occasion of our public sittings to see the evidences of ill health in a group of men who were the finest physical specimens in the country when they enlisted. It is of course difficult to measure good health or ill health by a casual inspection. There is one test of ill health, however, that is observable. The teeth of the veterans whom we saw were in a deplorable condition. How good health could possibly be retained with such poor teeth is difficult to understand.
It was perfectly obvious to us without being told-though we were told it on many occasions -that these veterans could not afford the dental treatment they needed. Certainly they could not afford the new sets of teeth that were dictated in most instances. Yet it was equally obvious to us that the country could not afford the physical deterioration resulting from these bad teeth.
I throw out that suggestion to the minister, that he give serious consideration to the question of treatment.
Another feature of this bill is that while it covers some of the South African veterans, it does not, as I understand, cover any Canadians who were domiciled in Canada before the South African war and who went to England and enlisted with the imperial forces there, nor does it cover soldiers who came to Canada for the first time after the South African war, although they may have been domiciled here since 1903 or 1904; the bill merely covers Canadians who served in a Canadian contingent in the South African war.
This bill will place on the war veterans' allowance board serious responsibilities. At present they have a very wide discretion; but by the bill they will be given even wider discretion, which means that their task will be much more difficult. In fairness to them I should like to say that in my short experience in public life I have never come across a board or a governmental authority which has
War Veterans' Allowance Act

received so much favourable comment. On every side one hears that this board, under Mr. Walter S. Woods and his associates, is doing splendid work. I should like here to pay tribute to the members for that work; they are rendering splendid service to this country, and I believe they may be relied upon to exercise in a satisfactory manner the increased discretion given them in this bill.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
Some of the remarks of the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Green) would perhaps have been more applicable in the discussion in committee. But since he has introduced them and as it is nearly six o'clock, may I add a word which perhaps the minister will consider during recess. Subsection 3 of section 4 reads:
An allowance shall not be awarded or continued under this act to a veteran or a recipient while such veteran or recipient is in receipt of an old age pension. . . .
The point I would like to make is this: A war veteran if married is entitled to $40 a month; but an old age pension is limited to $20, unless the man's wife also has an old age pension, and it would be unfair, as the hon. member suggested, if the attitude were adopted of compelling them on reaching the age of seventy to go under the Old Age Pensions Act, in which case their pension would be dropped from $40 to $20 a month.
There is one other point I should like to mention. It is not in criticism, but I should like the minister to confirm the apparent meaning of this section. I remember some years ago when a somewhat similar bill was up, dealing, I think, with the soldier settlers; there appeared to me to be some ambiguity in the language, and I asked the minister, with his deputy before him, whether the words in the bill meant so and so, which appeared to be the favourable interpretation. The minister assured me most emphatically that it was so. Six months later when I tried to see that the act was enforced in that way, that same deputy assured me that he was under no obligation whatever to pay any attention to anything the minister had said in the house, that he was guided solely by the legal meaning, and he entirely repudiated the meaning which the minister had positively given in the house. It may be my suspicious nature, but I am not quite clear whether the language used in paragraph (c) of section 4 is definite enough. It says that they will give this award to those who are:
. . . incapable and unlikely to become capable of maintaining himself because of economic handicaps combined with physical or mental disability or insufficiency.

The old section read:
. . . permanently unemployable by reason of physical or mental disability.
We always run up against this case; we would say to the board: "This man is incapable and permanently unemployable." They would say: "No, he is not; he could run an elevator." Perhaps the man was a logger or something. They would say: "Oh, well; this man could do something; he could flag a train at a railway crossing." They could always see some possible situation in which a man, unless absolutely bedridden, could do something, disregarding the fact that a logger could not become a bank clerk or something of that kind, and elevator jobs are very few. And we wanted the term introduced-I think it was introduced later-"economic disability"; but still it is a little vague. I should like the minister, if he could, to assure us after eight o'clock that that provision, "economic handicaps combined with physical or mental disability," will positively mean what it appears to mean, and we shall not have to prove that a man is almost bedridden before we can get him this award; otherwise very little benefit will result over the old act. The words, "economic handicaps combined with physical or mental disability," might compel the man to prove he was practically bedridden.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext: He could be a member of parliament.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
May I point out to the minister that in making the two appointments to the board he has undertaken a grave responsibility. These are important positions, carrying salaries of $6,000, and I ha ve heard it suggested that the appointments should be made by the civil service commission. I do not urge that, but I would emphasize the extreme importance of maintaining in this board the same humane disposition in dealing with cases coming before it that has been manifested in the past. Needless to say, the men to be appointed will have to be capable, and will have to possess qualities of the head. But it is essential that they have, too, qualities of the heart, because particularly in dealing with returned soldiers' legislation a great deal depends upon the administration of the act.
There have been items of war veteran legislation, the utility of which have been entirely destroyed by a too technical administration and interpretation of certain provisions. I hope when appointing two new members to the board the minister will dismiss from his mind all political considerations, and install men who will make their first consideration

War Veterans' Allowance Act
the welfare of the veteran. Most emphatically, the appointees should be returned men, men who have had a reasonable amount of service in the line. This is not a job for staff officers, unless they have had considerable regimental duty as well. There is no man so well qualified to deal with the veteran as one who has shared 'his hardships and his problems.
May I remind the minister of something he knows very well: the veteran will stand discomfort and hardship, privation and danger quite cheerfully, but he will not put up with what he describes as being chevied about. Under that heading fall all sorts of technical refinements, that disposition to introduce a mass of precedents in dealing with returned soldier legislation, which has been regrettably present in the attitude of certain other boards and commissions dealing with returned soldier legislation but not, I repeat, in connection with the war veterans' allowance board.
I should like to have seen in this legislation some provisions entitling those who draw the allowance, but who are not in receipt of a pension, to treatment and hospitalization in departmental hospitals. Perhaps that is something which may come later on in the session. I should like to see a provision for the payment of transportation costs of applicants to the nearest points at which they can be examined. As to the general purpose of the bill, may I quote from the minister's remarks in the debate on the resolution. At page 1039 of Hansard he is reported as follows:
It may be said that in passing this legislation we shall be fulfilling to the utmost the requests of the returned soldiers themselves as expressed through the dominion convention of the Canadian legion held in Port William early in February when a resolution was passed on the subject of cash bonus to veterans of the great *war. The resolution reads in part:
"That this convention endorse the resolution, passed by the dominion executive council to the effect that it is unalterably opposed to the principle of any bonus for service in the great war, conceiving it to be the responsibility of the government of Canada to adequately provide only for those disabled as a result of war service and dependents and dependents of the fallen and to ensure adequate assistance for those who saw service in a theatre of actual war and who are now by reason of economic conditions combined with their disability, tangible and intangible, resulting from war service, unable through no fault of their own to secure employment."
I am not going to discuss the matter fully, because I believe my remarks might be more appropriate in committee under section 4 of the bill. May I go on record now, however, as submitting that as it now stands section 4 will have to be drastically revised if the intention of the resolution passed by the
legion convention is to be carried out. At present I shall not go farther than that.
I should like to add my words of congratulation to what has been said, subject to a revision of section 4, which would bring the measure entirely in line with the minister's remarks I have just quoted.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because I welcome this bill I do not propose at this stage to speak at length upon it or to indulge in any carping criticism. I believe the measure will receive general commendation. I speak at this time rather because I fear that certain restrictive provisions in the bill may tend to impair its general usefulness. I desire io give the minister full credit for his intentions with regard to this measure, but I believe it is only proper to point out that the parliamentary inquiry of 1936 proved conclusively the necessity for such a measure. I think we should not overlook the fact that the two years' delay in caring for a certain category of veteran has meant growing misery and harrowing insecurity for the men in this category.
I am at a loss to understand why we should always have to wait until conditions become most acute before remedial legislation is introduced. I feel sure that such a policy will result in additional cost to the country as well as increased suffering and misery for those affected. If we review the history of legislation dealing with ex-service men, I think we shall find that the rather grudging attitude taken toward legislation of this kind has increased the ultimate cost. We should keep this experience in mind as we try to bring legislation of this sort to its final stage. I am particularly anxious, if we accept responsibility for the category of ex-service men as defined in this bill, that we should make certain that the responsibility is adequately and justly discharged. As I say, I have a definite fear that certain restrictions in the bill may detract from the reception it will receive from ex-service men in general.
I should like to refer particularly to the sections of the bill dealing with those who served in the South African war. As has been pointed out by preceding speakers, the benefits are limited to those who served in the Canadian contingents. I am bound to bring to the attention of the house the large number of
War Veterans' Allowance Act

men who served in the imperial units during the South African war and who very shortly after their periods of service established domiciles in Canada and have been residents of Canada continuously since that time. They have become closely identified with our national life and our national enterprises, and it seems unfair to discriminate against them in a measure of this kind. I should like to direct attention to this additional fact, that a large percentage of those who served in imperial units during t'he South African war enlisted for service in the great war of 1914-1918.

just what class of veterans who served in South Africa will be covered by this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
As is well known to hon. members, the War Veterans' Allowance Act heretofore restricted the veterans' allowance to those who served in the great war. This section extends the act to veterans who served in the Canadian contingents in South Africa during the hostilities commencing on October 11, 1899, and ending on May 31, 1902. Representations were made before the parliamentary committee of 1936, and again during the last session of parliament, among others by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I told him at that time that there might be certain difficulties, but that I would go into the matter thoroughly in an endeavour to bring these men under the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
As has already been suggested, a goodly percentage of these Canadians who served in the South African war served also in the great war, so they would in any case be eligible under the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. As to the exact number, we had some discussion about that last year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
That is just what I was
about to ask the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
I am able to say this:
There were 7,366 veterans who left Canada in the Canadian contingents for South Africa. Only 5,325 of these saw service on land during the campaign, the rest having arrived
subsequently to the cessation of hostilities and many of them never landing in South Africa at all. After deducting mortality from this 5,325, we estimate those now living to number approximately 3,500, and it is believed that at least half of these saw service also in the great war-this, of course, is only an estimate- and would therefore have entitlement under the act as at present. That would leave 1,750, of whom it is doubted if more than ten per cent are indigent and unprovided for, so that the total to be looked after by this amendment would not be more than 200 to 250. The expenditure is estimated to be from $30,000 to $35,000.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister in reference to a case I know of, that of a Canadian-born who served in the South African war and went with the corps to the relief of Mafeking, where Baden-Powell was besieged. This man came to see me a few days ago, and in the course of conversation told me his story. I am not sure that I can relate it with an absolutely clear understanding of all he said, but I understood him to say that after he reached South Africa he was transferred-he was in "C" battery

to Rhodesia. I assume he was transferred to some imperial corps. Would that soldier be qualified under this amendment? After he came back he studied for a doctor, and then went west to practise. He is now over sixty years of age, and has been back in Toronto for many years and is destitute. I was wondering if his being present at the relief of Mafeking would make him eligible for the war veterans' allowance.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD

speechtext: Thank you.

I think I can explain
that to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). After the siege of Mafeking Rhodesia borrowed some artillery from the imperials, they took "C" battery from the Canadian forces, and those men went and served in protecting the border around Rhodesia, but they were still under Canadian pay and allowances.

speechtext: I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the phrase, "theatre of actual war" and the interpretation placed upon it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
In connection with South
Africa?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext: It appears in the explanation in connection with the bill. The case I desire to draw to the minister's attention has to do with the great war, but the same phrase is used with regard to the South African veteran. The War Veterans' Allowance Act sets out quite clearly what "theatre of war" -was intended to mean, but as soon as the board undertook the administration of this act it was necessary to have a closer definition of what "theatre of war" meant with regard to the act. What I say is in no sense a criticism of the board. Rather would I associate myself with the well-chosen words of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) this afternoon in appreciation of the work that the board has done. Cases have arisen, not many in number, which do not seem to me to be receiving the intent of parliament-shall I put it in that way? The particular case I drew to the board's attention was that of a man who was on the strength of the military police at Folkestone. He was sent over to France in 1917, to carry out certain duties entrusted to him with regard to the election. I am told that others who were sent on similar duties actually were killed.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext: Some of us think they should have been.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
Possibly, but I was not for a moment looking at the matter from a partisan point of view. There seems little doubt that the car this particular man used was demolished by a direct hit. True, he was not in it. He has now come to a physical and financial disability, and his age is such that there is no question, I think, of his being eligible but for the fact that he does not come within the definition laid down by the Department of Justice. That definition is that to come within the category of those who served in a theatre of actual war a man must have been on the strength of a unit that was so serving. I was present in the house when this statute was passed, and it does not seem to me that that case is receiving what parliament intended such cases to receive.
I am told there are one or two other cases, not many in number I believe. There was one of a man sent over on conducting duties, and another of a man sent over on post office
CMr. Power.]
duties, and he was actually wounded, but he does not receive the benefits of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. I would draw the attention of the minister to these cases rather with the request that he should see whether, if they are not numerous-and I understand that they are not-they could not be brought within the meaning of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext: I am familiar with the cases submitted by my hon. friend. The particular case he mentions is one of those borderline cases that are very difficult to deal with, very much like the case of the conducting officer. There may be some discussion between us as to whether the man was actually serving at the front when he was engaged in the work of a political campaign-

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext: He was carrying out the duties he was sent there to perform.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext: I assume he was employed by the government, and not by a political party. I take that for granted.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext: I assume that.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext:
I take that for granted. In any case the whole question turns on the interpretation of the term, "service in a theatre of actual war." As my hon. friend has pointed out, the fact is that the Department of Justice has ruled that conducting officers could not properly speaking be said to have served in a theatre of actual war, and for that reason it ruled that they were not eligible under the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. I do not know that anything can be done about the matter. I would hesitate to propose an amendment which would still further enlarge this definition of service; it might allow eligibility to a very large number of persons for whom it was never intended that there should be provision in legislation such as this. After all, it must not be forgotten that these men were not wounded in the discharge of their military duties. People coming under this act are those whose disability cannot be attributed to their war service. They did not necessarily suffer injury or disability at the front; their disabilities are post war or such as may be assumed to be due to the war, owing to the strain and hardships which they underwent. It is perhaps difficult to imagine that a man whose duty was purely a civilian one such as that of a returning officer in an election would be put to any strain or hardship comparable with that of those who saw actual service in the trenches. However, I have no objection to giving consideration to the case submitted by my hon. friend.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF ALLOWANCES TO INCLUDE CERTAIN OTHER CLASSES-ENLARGEMENT OF MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD
speechtext: Would the minister give consideration to those who served in the South African campaign as members of imperial units and who established domicile in Canada almost immediately after the close of the campaign? As I endeavoured to point out before until I was reproved, if they have established twenty years' residence in Canada and are now over sixty years of age and in destitute circumstances, I see no reason why they should not be taken care of under this act, particularly as they no longer can establish even a remote claim in respect of the imperial government. They have been closely identified with our national life all this time, and I think it would be quite proper that they should be given consideration, particularly as many of them served in the Canadian expeditionary force and did valuable work and, because of the very fact that they gave such valuable service, were not allowed to proceed to France and are therefore excluded from the benefits of this legislation.
